semantic_correction.stem: An adult newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes says, ‘My vision is fine, so I don’t think I need an eye examination.’ Which response by the nurse is best?

options.A: Arrange an initial dilated comprehensive eye examination now because type 2 diabetes can already have clinically important retinopathy without visual symptoms.
options.B: Schedule the eye examination at the first annual diabetes follow-up if vision remains normal, because immediate screening is mainly needed when symptoms develop.
options.C: Begin retinopathy screening if A1C remains above target after treatment, because normal vision makes important retinal disease unlikely at diagnosis.
options.D: Use routine visual-acuity screening now and arrange a dilated examination if the acuity changes, because an asymptomatic client can wait for specialist screening.

semantic_correction.rationale: The 2026 American Diabetes Association Standards of Care recommend that people with type 2 diabetes have an initial dilated and comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist at the time of the diabetes diagnosis. ADA explains that type 2 diabetes may have been present for years before diagnosis and that clinically important or vision-threatening retinopathy may be asymptomatic. Therefore A is correct. B incorrectly delays screening until a later annual visit or symptoms. C creates an unsupported A1C-based trigger and incorrectly treats normal vision as evidence against retinopathy. D substitutes visual-acuity monitoring for the recommended initial comprehensive dilated examination and delays appropriate screening.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Teach adults with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes that diabetic retinopathy screening begins at diagnosis with an initial dilated comprehensive eye examination even when vision is normal because important retinal disease may be asymptomatic.
semantic_correction.source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes
semantic_correction.source_document_title: 12. Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
semantic_correction.source_version_date: Diabetes Care 2026;49(Supplement 1):S261–S276; published December 8, 2025; primary article rechecked August 20, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: Recommendation 12.4: people with type 2 diabetes should have an initial dilated and comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist at the time of the diabetes diagnosis. Screening discussion and Type 2 Diabetes subsection: vision-threatening retinopathy may be asymptomatic; type 2 diabetes may have had undiagnosed hyperglycemia for years and can have prevalent retinopathy at diagnosis; prompt diagnosis enables timely intervention.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: Newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes warrants an initial dilated comprehensive eye examination at diagnosis, and normal vision or absence of symptoms does not exclude clinically important diabetic retinopathy.
semantic_correction.blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
semantic_correction.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance, printed p.9 (official PDF pageno 12): prevention and/or early detection of health problems; perform targeted screening assessments (e.g., vision, nutrition, depression); educate client about preventive care and health maintenance recommendations; provide care and education for adult clients.
semantic_correction.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — diabetic retinopathy screening and early detection
semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup retained the retinopathy-screening-at-diagnosis construct, removed the original only/always cueing, rebuilt A/B/C/D as plausible competing screening strategies, and shortened the key so it is not uniquely longest.

scope_exclusions.subsequent_interval: The item tests the initial examination at diagnosis; it does not require a later screening interval after one or more normal examinations.
scope_exclusions.retinal_photography: Remote retinal photography and FDA-authorized AI screening are not tested; the item focuses on the ADA-recommended initial dilated comprehensive examination.
scope_exclusions.symptoms: The absence of visual symptoms does not rule out retinopathy; the item does not imply that new visual symptoms should wait for routine screening.
scope_exclusions.glycemic_control: No A1C threshold or glucose target determines whether the initial eye examination is due at type 2 diabetes diagnosis.
scope_exclusions.treatment: The item does not test retinal treatment, anti-VEGF therapy, laser therapy, pregnancy-related screening, or ophthalmology follow-up after retinopathy is found.
scope_exclusions.provider_role: The nurse reinforces and coordinates the recommended screening; the comprehensive dilated examination is performed by an ophthalmologist or optometrist.

option_audit.A: Correct. It matches ADA Recommendation 12.4 and explains why normal vision does not remove the need for screening at diagnosis.
option_audit.B: Plausible because many preventive services are annual, but the first eye examination in type 2 diabetes is due at diagnosis rather than deferred until the first annual follow-up.
option_audit.C: Plausible because glycemic control affects retinopathy risk, but ADA does not make elevated A1C a prerequisite for the initial screening examination.
option_audit.D: Plausible because visual acuity is part of eye assessment, but it cannot replace or delay the recommended initial dilated comprehensive examination.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. A alone gives the correct timing and screening method. B delays screening, C invents an A1C trigger, and D substitutes a narrower assessment for the recommended initial comprehensive examination.

cueing_check.note: The key is not longest; all four are complete screening/teaching responses with comparable length and no only/all/always/never/every cue.

blueprint_audit.entry_level_relevance: NCSBN Health Promotion and Maintenance explicitly includes targeted vision screening and education about preventive care and early detection, directly supporting this entry-level RN screening-teaching construct.
